subject: English
board: KS3 English (school curriculum), leading to International GCSE English Language and English Literature
source: Drive English KS3 3yr Scheme of Work (Year 8 War Poetry unit: Owen, Rosenberg, McCrae, Brooke) adapted; National Curriculum KS3 English; assessment objectives aligned to AQA GCSE English Language 8700 and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature 4ET1. Poems are public domain, quoted briefly; all models are teacher-written originals.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: War poetry - context and persuasion
lessons.title: Why war poetry? The First World War in context
objectives: Describe key facts about the First World War and trench life
Build a lexical field (word bank) for war
Explain why people write poetry about conflict

keywords.def: a long narrow ditch dug as a shelter for soldiers
the main battle line in France and Belgium, 1914-1918
a group of words linked by one topic
the background of time, place and events around a text
the agreement that ended fighting on 11 November 1918

starter: Bismillah. Name two features of an autobiography.
Define hyperbole and give an example.
What is a noun phrase? Write one.

teach.heading: The First World War
bullets: Fought from 1914 to 1918
Millions of soldiers from many countries took part
Fighting on the Western Front was in trenches
Armistice: 11 November 1918
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask: ‘What do you already know about the First World War?’ Take responses on a shared board. Explain that Britain's army was first made up of volunteers, and from 1916 conscription (compulsory service) was introduced. Many Indian soldiers, including many Muslims, fought on the Western Front. Link to Remembrance Day: 11 November falls in our second week of term, so we will remember with respect.

teach.heading: Life in the trenches
bullets: Mud, rats and lice
Noise of shells and gunfire
Danger of gas attacks
Fear, boredom, loss and comradeship
teach.note: Show two or three images (teacher-chosen archive photographs from the Imperial War Museums). Ask pupils to write three words about each image. Handle sensitively: no graphic images. Explain that soldiers waited long hours in trenches between attacks. Ask: ‘Which emotions might they feel?’

teach.heading: What is a lexical field?
bullets: Words linked by one topic
War field: shell, trench, bayonet, rifle
Emotion field: dread, grief, courage
Poets choose lexical fields to create mood
teach.note: Model building a word bank in three columns: sights, sounds, feelings. Pupils add words in chat for 2 minutes. Keep the bank: it will be used in lessons 2, 3 and 7. Misconception: a lexical field is just any adjectives. It must share a topic.

teach.heading: Why poetry?
bullets: Poems pack feeling into few words
Poets were also soldiers
They wanted to tell the truth, remember, or persuade
Readers still read them today
teach.note: Explain war poets were often young soldiers writing in the middle of the experience. Poetry compresses emotions. Ask: ‘Why might someone write a poem and not a letter?’ Link to Islamic ethos: Qur'an 5:32 teaches that taking one innocent life is as if one had killed all of humanity, and saving one life is as if saving all of humanity. We study these poems in order to understand the human cost of war and to pray for peace.

practice: Add five words to each column of the word bank: sights / sounds / feelings.
True or false: (a) The war ended in 1918. (b) Conscription began in 1914. (c) Trenches were on the Western Front. Correct the false one.
Why might a poet choose the word ‘shrieking’ rather than ‘loud’ to describe a shell?
independent: Write six sentences describing a trench using at least eight words from your word bank. Include one simile.
Explain in three sentences why Remembrance Day matters.
Extension: write one sentence that tells a reader how it feels to wait in a trench using a lexical field of silence.
exit: What is a lexical field? Give one example from the war.
Give two reasons why poets wrote about war.
lessons.homework: Find out what the red poppy represents and write four sentences explaining its link to Remembrance Day.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-filled word bank with pictures. EAL: translate key terms and use cognates. Stretch: research the contribution of Muslim soldiers in the war and write a short paragraph.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: War poetry - context and persuasion
lessons.title: Persuading men to fight: recruitment posters and radio adverts
objectives: Identify persuasive techniques in recruitment propaganda
Use imperatives and direct address accurately
Write a recruitment poster or radio advert

keywords.def: information used to push people to think or act in a certain way
a command verb, e.g. Join!
speaking to the reader as ‘you’
words chosen to make the reader feel strongly
the people the text is aimed at

starter: Give three words from our war word bank.
What was the Western Front?
Define lexical field.

teach.heading: What is propaganda?
bullets: Messages designed to change beliefs or actions
Often one-sided
Used heavily to recruit soldiers in 1914
Posters, newspapers, songs and speeches
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain propaganda is not always lies but it is selective. In 1914 the British government and others used posters to encourage men to volunteer. Ask: ‘Do adverts today try to persuade you in the same way?’ Link to the importance of checking sources and seeking truth, which is also part of media literacy.

teach.heading: A famous poster
bullets: 1914: Lord Kitchener, ‘Your Country Needs You’
Pointing finger and direct stare
Imperative and direct address
Makes the reader feel responsible
teach.note: Show the well-known poster (teacher selects from Imperial War Museums archive). Ask: ‘Where is Kitchener looking? How does it make you feel?’ Identify direct address (‘you’) and the pointing finger. Misconception: persuasion always uses facts. Often it uses feeling and pressure.

teach.heading: Persuasive toolkit
bullets: Imperatives: Join! Fight! Be there!
Pronouns: you, your, we, our
Emotive language: duty, honour, shame
Rule of three and short sentences
teach.note: Create the toolkit together on a board. Practise writing one imperative sentence in 30 seconds on a topic, e.g. ‘Join the school's recycling team’. Pupils share. Then apply the same techniques to the history topic. Point out the contrast between persuasive words and what the poets later reveal.

teach.heading: Writing in role
bullets: Poster: a short, bold message and a slogan
Radio advert: speak directly, add sound effects
Open letter: describe the reality of the trenches
Think carefully about audience and purpose
teach.note: Explain two tasks: (1) a recruitment poster or radio advert from the perspective of 1914; (2) a contrasting open letter from a soldier in the trenches warning men what it is really like. Pupils choose one today and the other for homework. Reiterate that we are writing in a historical role to understand the techniques, not to promote violence.

practice: Highlight imperatives and direct address in: ‘Men of Britain! Join your friends today. Your family needs you. Do not delay!’
Add emotive language to this plain slogan: ‘Join the army.’
Rewrite the same slogan as a persuasion for the school football team using two imperatives and the pronoun ‘you’.
independent: Write the text for a 1914 recruitment poster or a 30-second radio advert for volunteers. Use at least three imperatives, direct address, one emotive word and a slogan of 6 words or fewer.
Annotate your text with the techniques used.
Extension: write a one-sentence counter-slogan from a soldier already at the front.
exit: Name two persuasive techniques used in recruitment posters.
What is the effect of the pronoun ‘you’?
lessons.homework: Write an open letter (120 words) from a soldier in the trenches to a young man thinking about joining up, using your lexical field word bank.
lessons.send: SEND: give a scaffold with sentence starters for each technique. EAL: pre-teach imperative verbs with pictures. Stretch: analyse how modern adverts use the same techniques.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: War poetry - reading the poems
lessons.title: Anthem for Doomed Youth (Wilfred Owen): sound and imagery
objectives: Identify imagery and sound techniques in the poem
Explain how the sonnet structure shapes meaning
Write an analytical paragraph using evidence

keywords.def: a 14-line poem, often with a change of focus after line 8
a word that sounds like what it describes, e.g. rattle
giving human qualities to a non-human thing
a comparison using like or as
when the meaning is the opposite of what is expected

starter: Name two propaganda techniques.
What is an imperative? Give one.
Which word in our word bank best shows fear?

teach.heading: Meet the poet
bullets: Wilfred Owen: British soldier and poet
Wrote about what he saw on the Western Front
Killed on 4 November 1918, a week before the Armistice
Most poems published after his death
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the poem aloud once, slowly. Ask pupils what they notice before explaining anything. Cite the poem's opening: ‘What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?’ A passing-bell is a church bell rung when someone has died. Ask: ‘Why does the poet ask a question?’

teach.heading: The title and the question
bullets: ‘Anthem’ is a song of celebration
‘Doomed’ means certain to die
Irony: a joyful word with a grim one
Opening question pulls the reader in
teach.note: Discuss why Owen pairs ‘anthem’ with ‘doomed’. Explain irony. Ask: ‘What would a proper funeral involve? What do these soldiers get instead?’ Misconception: ‘doomed’ means the soldiers are bad. It means fated to die.

teach.heading: Sound techniques
bullets: ‘Only the monstrous anger of the guns’
Personification: guns have anger
‘stuttering rifles' rapid rattle’
Onomatopoeia and alliteration of r and t
teach.note: Read the lines aloud and have pupils tap the rhythm of ‘rifles' rapid rattle’. Explain that the repeated r and t sounds copy gunfire. Ask: ‘Why does the poet make the guns sound angry, not just loud?’ Possible: war as a monstrous force. Practice naming the effect: it makes war seem violent and unstoppable.

teach.heading: Sonnet structure
bullets: Lines 1-8: the battlefield
Lines 9-14: the home front
‘The pallor of girls' brows shall be their pall’
‘Each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds’
teach.note: Explain a sonnet has 14 lines. Owen shifts from the noise of the battlefield to the quiet grief at home: families closing their blinds. Note the contrast between loud and silent. Ask: ‘Which part feels sadder to you, and why?’ Link to our own sense of mourning with dignity and prayer, while the poem says there are no ‘mockeries’ of proper rituals for these men.

teach.heading: Writing about the poem
bullets: Point: Owen presents war as…
Evidence: short quotation
Explain: the word … suggests …
Link back to the question
teach.note: Model one paragraph: ‘Owen presents the guns as angry and cruel. The phrase ‘monstrous anger’ personifies the guns, suggesting war is a beast that destroys young lives. This makes the reader feel horror and pity.’ Then ask pupils to improve it by commenting on the word ‘monstrous’ in more depth.

practice: Find and name one example each of onomatopoeia, personification and a simile in lines 1-4.
Why might Owen end the poem with a quiet image of blinds being drawn rather than another loud sound?
Write the evidence part of a PEE paragraph using the quotation ‘die as cattle’. What does it suggest about how the soldiers are treated?
independent: Write a paragraph (6-8 sentences) answering: How does Owen present the horror of war in the first eight lines? Include two short quotations.
Underline the technique name and the effect in your paragraph.
Extension: write two sentences on how the structure shifts in lines 9-14.
exit: What is a sonnet? How does Owen use the second half of this one?
Give one example of personification from the poem and explain its effect.
lessons.homework: Learn lines 1-4 of the poem and be ready to read them aloud with expression.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a glossary (orisons, pall) and a paragraph frame. EAL: audio recording and line-by-line paraphrase. Stretch: compare to a modern poem about conflict.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: War poetry - reading the poems
lessons.title: Break of Day in the Trenches (Isaac Rosenberg): the rat and the poet's tone
objectives: Explain how a symbol (the rat) conveys ideas
Identify tone and how it changes
Infer the poet's message from imagery

keywords.def: something that stands for a bigger idea
the attitude a writer shows, e.g. bitter, calm, ironic
mocking in a bitter way
poetry without a regular rhyme or rhythm pattern
placing two contrasting things side by side

starter: What is irony in the title ‘Anthem for Doomed Youth’?
Name a sound technique Owen uses.
Write a PEE sentence about the word ‘monstrous’.

teach.heading: Introducing Rosenberg
bullets: Isaac Rosenberg: soldier-poet from London
Wrote the poem in 1916
Killed in action in 1918
Poem is set at dawn in the trenches
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the poem aloud. Rosenberg was from a Jewish immigrant family in the East End of London, and a private soldier, not an officer. Mention that poets from varied backgrounds wrote about the war. Cite the opening: ‘The darkness crumbles away.’ Ask: ‘What does ‘crumbles’ suggest about the darkness?’

teach.heading: The rat as a symbol
bullets: ‘A queer sardonic rat’ crosses both sides
Rats move freely; soldiers cannot
‘Cosmopolitan sympathies’: at home everywhere
The poet speaks to the rat
teach.note: Explain the rat touches the hand of a British soldier and will also touch German hands. The poet jokes that the rat would be shot if anyone knew its ‘cosmopolitan sympathies’. Ask: ‘What is the poet saying about borders and enemies?’ Possible: nature does not care for boundaries; ordinary soldiers on both sides share the same danger.

teach.heading: Tone and contrast
bullets: Calm morning against deadly danger
Joking tone: ‘Droll rat’
Darker tone: ‘shrieking iron and flame’
Juxtaposition of the playful and the deadly
teach.note: Ask pupils to trace the tone through the poem with a line graph (calm to bitter to sorrowful). Show that the poem is quiet but unsettling. Explain the key line: ‘Poppies whose roots are in man's veins / Drop, and are ever dropping’, which links poppies, red like blood, to dying soldiers. Misconception: that the poppies are only a pretty image. They signal death.

teach.heading: Form and message
bullets: Free verse: no regular rhyme
Lines vary in length like uneasy thoughts
No heroic language at all
Message: all soldiers share the same fear
teach.note: Compare with Owen's sonnet. Discuss why free verse might suit a poem about uncertainty. Ask: ‘Does Rosenberg glorify war?’ Elicit evidence: no. Write a class sentence together: ‘Rosenberg presents the soldiers as ordinary and vulnerable, as shown by…’.

practice: Explain ‘cosmopolitan sympathies’ in your own words. What does the rat have that the soldiers do not?
Identify the contrast between ‘the darkness crumbles away’ and ‘shrieking iron and flame’. What mood does each create?
Complete: The image of poppies with roots ‘in man's veins’ suggests…
independent: Write a paragraph (6-8 sentences): How does Rosenberg use the rat to present ideas about war? Include two short quotations and explain effect.
Draw a tone graph for the poem and label three key words.
Extension: write two sentences explaining why Rosenberg avoids rhyme.
exit: What does a symbol do in a poem?
Give one word that describes the tone of Rosenberg's poem and justify it.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-line diary entry from the point of view of the rat, as it crosses No Man's Land at dawn.
lessons.send: SEND: provide an annotated copy with key phrases highlighted. EAL: glossary for ‘droll’, ‘sardonic’, ‘druid’. Stretch: compare Rosenberg's and Owen's views about who is responsible for suffering.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: War poetry - reading the poems
lessons.title: In Flanders Fields (John McCrae): the voice of the dead
objectives: Describe the form and refrain of the poem
Explain the effect of the speakers and their message
Discuss the tension between grief and encouragement to fight on

keywords.def: a French poetic form with a repeated refrain and a set rhyme pattern
a line or phrase repeated in a poem
a command verb
the voice that tells the poem
something that stands for a bigger idea

starter: What is the symbol in Rosenberg's poem?
Define free verse.
Give one example of juxtaposition.

teach.heading: The poem's background
bullets: John McCrae: a Canadian doctor and soldier
Written in May 1915 near Ypres
Published in Punch in December 1915
Inspired the red remembrance poppy
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the poem aloud. Explain McCrae wrote it after the death of a friend in the Second Battle of Ypres. Ask: ‘Why do poppies grow in the battlefield?’ (disturbed soil). Link to Remembrance: poppies are worn in November in Britain. Handle sensitively; some pupils may have family who served.

teach.heading: Who is speaking?
bullets: ‘We are the Dead.’
The speakers are fallen soldiers
‘Short days ago / We lived, felt dawn’
Ordinary life stopped suddenly
teach.note: Cite plainly: ‘We are the Dead. Short days ago / We lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow, / Loved and were loved’. Ask: ‘How does it feel to hear from the dead?’ Possible: shocking, sad, powerful. Highlight the short sentences and the plain verbs of everyday life.

teach.heading: Form and refrain
bullets: Rondeau: a repeated opening phrase returns as a refrain
‘In Flanders fields’ ends every verse
Regular rhyme gives a steady rhythm
Repetition keeps the dead in our minds
teach.note: Explain a rondeau repeats an opening phrase as a refrain. Ask: ‘What does the repetition do?’ Possible: like a memorial chant, rhythm of a lament. Pupils clap the rhyme pattern. Contrast with Rosenberg's free verse.

teach.heading: The final demand
bullets: ‘Take up our quarrel with the foe’
Imperative: the dead command the living
‘The torch; be yours to hold it high’
Threat: ‘If ye break faith with us who die’
teach.note: Discuss the final stanza. The dead ask the living to continue the fight. Ask: ‘Is this a comfort or a pressure?’ Explain that readers have debated this poem: some see it as a call to honour the dead, others as pressure to keep fighting. Encourage balanced views. Mention that the poem was used in appeals for war bonds in Canada.

practice: Find two details of ordinary life that the dead mention. What do they make the reader feel?
Underline the imperatives in the final stanza. What is the effect of using commands?
‘If ye break faith with us who die’: what does ‘break faith’ mean?
independent: Write a paragraph (6-8 sentences) answering: How does McCrae use the voice of the dead to affect the reader? Include two short quotations.
Draw the rhyme pattern of the first verse, labelling the refrain.
Extension: write two sentences about whether the final stanza is comforting or demanding.
exit: What is a refrain and what is its effect in this poem?
Give one imperative from the poem and explain it.
lessons.homework: Write a four-line reply to the dead soldiers from a person living today, using at least one image of remembrance.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a verse-by-verse paraphrase. EAL: pronunciation help for ‘foe’ and ‘quarrel’. Stretch: debate whether the poem is propaganda or remembrance.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: War poetry - reading the poems
lessons.title: Two views of war: Brooke's The Soldier and Owen's Dulce et Decorum Est
objectives: Compare an idealised and a realistic view of war
Use comparative connectives accurately
Select short quotations from two poems

keywords.def: showing love and loyalty for your country
to present something as perfect or better than it is
showing things as they truly are
to explain similarities and differences
a word or phrase that links ideas, e.g. whereas

starter: What is a rondeau?
Which poem uses a rat as a symbol?
Define tone.

teach.heading: Rupert Brooke and The Soldier
bullets: Wrote it in 1914, at the start of the war
Died in 1915 of illness, not in battle
‘If I should die, think only this of me’
England is like a mother
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the first lines. Brooke's poem imagines a soldier who dies abroad but remains part of England: ‘some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England’. Ask: ‘What picture of death does this give?’ Possible: peaceful, noble. Make clear he wrote early, before the harshest trench fighting.

teach.heading: The language of The Soldier
bullets: ‘A body of England's, breathing English air’
Repetition of ‘England’ and ‘English’
Gentle images: rivers, suns, sounds
Death presented as a gift to the country
teach.note: Show how repeating ‘England’ and the soft sounds create a calm, proud tone. Ask: ‘Does the poem mention pain or fear?’ Pupils should notice it does not. Define idealise.

teach.heading: Owen's reality
bullets: Dulce et Decorum Est: gas attack scene
‘Bent double, like old beggars under sacks’
‘Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!’
‘The old Lie’ is the final target
teach.note: Use only short extracts and warn pupils the poem describes a soldier's suffering; stay respectful and calm. Explain the Latin line means ‘it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country’ and Owen calls it ‘the old Lie’. Ask: ‘Who is Owen angry with, and why?’ Possible: those who tell young people that war is glorious.

teach.heading: Comparing the poems
bullets: Both are about soldiers and death
Similarly, both use strong images
However, Brooke is calm and proud
Whereas Owen is angry and graphic
teach.note: Teach comparative connectives: similarly, likewise, however, in contrast, whereas, on the other hand. Model: ‘Brooke presents death as peaceful, whereas Owen presents it as a violent struggle.’ Misconception: pupils write about the poems in two separate halves. Weave them together in one sentence.

practice: Make a two-column table: Brooke / Owen. Complete rows for: tone, image of death, attitude to war, one short quotation.
Finish: ‘Brooke uses gentle images such as…, whereas Owen uses violent images such as…’
Which poem would work better as a recruitment text? Why?
independent: Write a comparison paragraph (7-9 sentences): How do Brooke and Owen present death in war differently? Use two quotations from each poem and at least three comparative connectives.
Highlight your connectives and check each pair of ideas is compared.
Extension: explain why the date of writing might change the poet's view.
exit: Give two comparative connectives and use one in a sentence.
Which poet is more realistic? Support your answer.
lessons.homework: Complete your comparison paragraph with one more quotation from each poem and bring it to the next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: use a comparison table and connectives bank. EAL: preview vocabulary ‘idealise’, ‘realistic’. Stretch: write a comparison of Brooke's calm tone with McCrae's urgent tone.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: War poetry - comparing and responding
lessons.title: Writing in role: a soldier's letter or monologue
objectives: Write in first person from the viewpoint of a soldier
Use a lexical field, imagery and varied punctuation
Control tense and tone to engage a reader

keywords.def: a long speech by one person
writing from the ‘I’ viewpoint
the writer's attitude or mood
a mark (-) that adds a pause or extra detail
three dots (...) showing a pause or something unsaid

starter: Define idealise.
Which poem uses a refrain?
Write a comparative sentence using ‘whereas’.

teach.heading: Writing in role
bullets: Choose a soldier: age, background, hopes
Choose an audience: mother, brother, friend
Choose a purpose: reassure, confess, warn
Keep to one clear voice
teach.note: Say bismillah. Model planning with a character: Tom, 19, from Leeds, writing to his younger sister. Pupils plan their own in three notes: who, to whom, why. Remind them it is a historical role, and we show respect to those who suffered. Ask: ‘What would he not tell his mother?’

teach.heading: Showing, not telling
bullets: Telling: ‘I was scared.’
Showing: ‘My hands would not stop shaking.’
Use senses: mud, cold, noise, smell
Use details from your word bank
teach.note: Compare telling and showing with several pairs. Ask pupils to convert ‘I was cold’. Use a sensory line: ‘The cold crept through my boots and settled in my bones.’ Link to poems: Owen and Rosenberg both show through images, not statements.

teach.heading: Punctuation for voice
bullets: Dash: ‘I wanted to speak - I could not.’
Ellipsis: ‘I wonder if you...’
Short sentences for tension
Exclamation sparingly for shock
teach.note: Explain how punctuation reflects a speaking voice. Dashes interrupt or add; ellipses trail off. Warn about overuse: one or two are enough. Model a paragraph: ‘Dearest Mary, the guns stopped at dawn - it was so quiet I could hear a bird. A bird! I had almost forgotten...’ Ask pupils which punctuation helps the voice.

teach.heading: Tense and tone
bullets: Past tense for events: ‘We marched’
Present tense for feelings now: ‘I am tired’
Keep the tone honest and personal
End with a hope or a question
teach.note: Explain that letters naturally move between past events and present feelings. Pupils must signal shifts clearly. Model a closing: ‘Say a prayer for me, as I do for you.’ Check tone: respectful, not graphic. Discuss that a good ending often returns to a human connection.

practice: Rewrite as ‘show, don’t tell’: ‘I was frightened and tired.’ Write two different versions.
Add a dash and an ellipsis to this sentence to improve voice: ‘I wanted to tell you but I could not find the words.’
Choose three words from the word bank to use in your opening line.
independent: Write a 10-12 sentence letter or monologue from a First World War soldier to someone at home. Use at least five words from your lexical field, one simile, a dash and an ellipsis.
Underline the sentences that show feelings rather than tell them.
Extension: include a short phrase echoing one of the poems, with a note explaining your choice.
exit: Why is ‘show, don't tell’ more powerful?
Write one sentence using a dash correctly.
lessons.homework: Finish your letter or monologue and proofread for tense, punctuation and spelling.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a letter frame with paragraph prompts. EAL: translate selected vocabulary and allow a drafted version in home language first. Stretch: write a second letter in reply.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: War poetry - comparing and responding
lessons.title: Writing about poems: PEE paragraphs, comparison and our own verse
objectives: Write a well-structured analytical paragraph with evidence and explanation
Compare two poems in a single response
Write an original short war or peace poem

keywords.def: Point, Evidence, Explain: a structure for analytical paragraphs
words copied exactly from a text, in speech marks
explaining how and why a writer's choices create effects
a group of lines in a poem
a central idea that runs through a text

starter: Name the war poet who wrote about a rat.
Give a comparative connective.
Define stanza.

teach.heading: The PEE paragraph
bullets: Point: answer the question directly
Evidence: a short quotation
Explain: what the word or technique suggests
Link: tie back to the question
teach.note: Say bismillah. Show a full model paragraph: ‘Owen presents war as cruel and unstoppable. He writes that ‘only the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle’ can speak for the dead, which suggests there is no human voice left to mourn them. The harsh sounds of ‘rapid rattle’ imitate gunfire, so the reader feels the noise of war. Overall, Owen shows that war silences humanity.’ Pupils identify P, E, E and L.

teach.heading: Using quotations well
bullets: Keep quotes short: 1-6 words
Put quotes in speech marks
Embed in your own sentence
Zoom in on one key word
teach.note: Show weak versus strong quotation use. Weak: copying a whole line without comment. Strong: embedding ‘monstrous anger’ and commenting on ‘monstrous’. Practise by cutting down long quotations on a list together. Common error: forgetting to explain after the quote.

teach.heading: Comparing in one paragraph
bullets: Start with one idea shared by both poems
Quote from poem A, then poem B
Use connectives: whereas, similarly
End with a judgement
teach.note: Model: ‘Both poets use strong images of death, but they are very different. Brooke writes of a ‘richer dust’, suggesting a noble sacrifice, whereas Owen describes ‘the old Lie’ to show that this idea is false.’ Ask pupils to improve a weak sentence. Ensure Brooke's quotation is checked against the class copy of the poem before using.

teach.heading: Writing our own verse
bullets: Choose a theme: remembrance or peace
Use a lexical field and one image
Try a refrain or a contrast
Keep to 8-12 lines
teach.note: Link to McCrae's refrain and Owen's contrasts. Model an original verse about peace, e.g. ‘The guns are quiet now. / Look - a bird sings on the wire. / Remember them. Speak peace.’ Emphasise we write respectfully. Invite pupils to share with the right to pass. End with a short dua for peace and for those who suffer in conflict today.

practice: Label the parts (P, E, E, L) in the model paragraph about Owen.
Cut this quotation to its key words: ‘What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?’ Choose 3-4 words and say why.
Write one comparative sentence about Brooke and Owen using ‘whereas’.
independent: Write a full PEE comparison paragraph answering: How do poets in this unit present the reality of war? Use two poems and at least three short quotations.
Self-assess with the checklist: point, short quotes, zoom in, comparison, link.
Write an 8-12 line original poem about remembrance or peace, using a lexical field and a refrain.
exit: What does the ‘E’ in PEE stand for? Give a sentence stem you can use.
Say one thing you learned about how poets use language.
lessons.homework: Redraft your comparison paragraph using feedback, and polish your poem to read aloud next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: provide paragraph scaffolds and word banks. EAL: model sentences with sentence starters. Stretch: write a second paragraph on a third poem from the unit.
